title: "That is a lot of work": Persona 4 Revival producer says there's no plans for a Yosuke romance option, even if the team did think about it
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Better luck next remake

While it's never been confirmed, some cut voice lines from the original release of Persona 4 indicated that once upon a time, the protagonist's right-hand party member Yosuke was romanceable. Instead what we ended up getting was a mostly quite homophobic character who never really moves past that mentality, though the upcoming Personal 4 Revival will apparently be changing Yosuke a bit. Though one thing it won't be doing, apparently, is adding that romance back in, even if the devs did consider it.

Speaking to GamesRadar about the requests for a romanceable Yosuke option in the remake, producer Kazuhisa Wada explained, "I was aware that some people were talking online about, like, 'Oh, Yosuke,' and they were kind of hoping for that. But we were thinking, if we did Yosuke, we kind of would have to do all the other male characters as well. And if we did that, that is a lot of work. So we were thinking about our time and schedule. I don't know if we could actually handle this, so we decided to let Yosuke float on by."

I'm certainly in two minds about this comment. On the one hand, it feels a touch like a cop out, as I don't even know why every main NPC has to be romanceable in the first place. On the other, I'm not sure I'd personally want a Yosuke romance. While Wada has admitted that Yosuke was "a little bit insensitive in terms of how he treats outsiders sometimes," and that the changes will make him fit better in "the world we live in now," I question what that means exactly.

Will he simply not be homophobic anymore? It's a quality quite baked into his character, and I'd rather a remake examine that and have his arc be more about confronting his bigoted opinions and apologising for the actions he took because of them. There is a general read on Yosuke that sees a lot of what he says as internalised homophobia too, but if the game were to just ignore he was ever like that and throw in a romance option, it would just feel like painting over a mouldy wall to me. Fingers crossed the changes feel natural at least.

title: Mortal Shell 2's latest update adds in an experimental new mode that adjusts the challenge based on how much you do or don't die
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Prepare to try and not die

Another week, another Mortal Shell 2 update! The first proper one arrived a week ago, and smoothed down some of the game's rough edges to make for a (slightly) more generous experience. This next update brings with it a bevy of changes, but most notably is an experimental adaptive difficulty mode that changes depending how well you're doing.

It's all pretty simple. At times when you're doing well, taking down baddies and bosses without a hitch, they start to get harder. "Enemies gain damage, health and break resist, so they hit harder, take longer to bring down and are more difficult to stagger," a Steam blog post explains. "Keep clearing encounters without dying and enemies will scale well past the toughest the game was originally built to be, and they will keep climbing for as long as you keep winning."

On the opposite end of things, if you keep dying, your foes will weaken. They'll inversely do less damage, have less health and resist, "and a cap is applied so that no single attack can take more than a set fraction of your health bar, meaning you cannot be killed outright from full health." If you're playing in Night Mode, it should be noted, "these reductions do not apply." You should also be made aware that there is no visual indicator to show whether the game has gotten easier or harder, but there are plans to add something in further down the line.

The update goes a bit further than that too, with it now being possible to apply status effects to enemies when they're sorting themselves out after a riposte. In terms of balance, the update has "improved the logic around Gloom drops on death, making it easier for players to retrieve their lost Gloom." You'll also find a plethora of bug fixes, performance adjustments, audio tweaks, and even a few story changes.

title: Snapchat takes aim at Partiful with new event-planning features
author: Aisha Malik
content:
Snapchat announced on Thursday that it’s launching “Snapchat Plans,” a suite of features for creating, sharing, and managing real-world events with friends. The new event-planning features allow users to send and receive invitations and track details like the time, location, and attendees, all in one place.

Snapchat says the new features can be used to organize everything from birthday celebrations and sporting events to study sessions and weekend hangouts.

With Snapchat Plans, the social network is looking to take on Partiful, a popular event planning and digital invitation platform, as young users turn to dedicated apps to organize get-togethers rather than relying on group chats or social media. Snapchat isn’t the only tech company taking on Partiful and other invitation apps, as Apple launched an app called Invites last year that lets users create custom invitations for any occasion.

Snapchat users can create an event, called a “Snapchat Plan,” by adding a title, choosing a date and time, and inviting up to 200 friends. Invitations are then delivered directly within a one-on-one chat with each invited friend. Guests can then RSVP with “Going,” “Maybe,” or “Can’t Go.”

The app is also adding a new “My Plans” section on users’ profiles that lets them quickly browse all of their current, upcoming, and past Snapchat Plans. Additionally, once users click on a friend’s profile, they will see the events they share with them.

Once a Snapchat Plan is created, hosts can see who’s attending, invite more friends, and update event details as needed. Guests can view the full guest list, change their RSVP at any time, and get a reminder one hour before the event starts.

Although Snapchat has been a significant player in the social media space over the past decade, the company is now expanding its focus beyond how people communicate online to also help shape how they get together in the real world. This follows the broader trend that sees Gen Z looking for more in-person connections.

“No more missed get-togethers because of buried messages, lost details, or forgetting to create an invitation,” the company wrote in a blog post. “Snapchat Plans make it easier to organize these special in-person moments with your friends.”

Snapchat Plans are private and invite-only, the company says.

title: Claude, Codex, and Hermes installed unowned code inside corporate networks
content:
Documentation files on more than 100 websites are referencing potentially dangerous executable content that gets installed automatically when visited by many AI agents. A few dozen companies, some of them Fortune 500s, are among those that executed proof-of-concept code. At least one misconfigured site is directing visitors, human or AI, to live malware.

The potentially dangerous content is in llms.txt and llms-full.txt files, an emerging convention websites employ to provide machine-readable summaries of the site’s content and its high-level structure. These files are the AI equivalent of the robots.txt standard that instructs search engines how to index the site’s content. Google Lighthouse, a tool for helping web developers, has more here. Correctly configured llms.txt and llms-full.txt files for Cloudflare are here and here.

How the researchers found it

Researchers at a stealth startup in Israel scanned 6,214 live domains belonging to defense contractors, Fortune 500, and Big Tech companies. Of the 8,265 llms.txt and llms-full.txt files they found (many sites hosted both an llms.txt and an llms-full.txt file), 120 of them, each on a different site, pointed to one or more code packages or domain names that weren’t registered. To test what happens when an AI agent processes such files, the researchers registered a handful of the unclaimed names and hosted packages that caused any machine executing them to reach out to their server. Within an hour, the researchers received a phone-home response from a Fortune 500 company. Over time, they got a few dozen more, some from more Fortune 500 companies and others from startups. Their beacon also recorded the chain of parent processes that spawned each install, ultimately revealing that coding agents, including Claude, OpenAI’s Codex, and Nous Research’s Hermes, were involved. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nous Research did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication.

“The trust model is broken,” Alon Hertz, one of the researchers, wrote in an interview. “Agents treat vendor docs as ground truth and don’t question them—and neither do the humans supervising them. Agentic AI usage is exploding, and agents are spreading across every layer—SaaS, cloud, endpoint. As they multiply, so does the supply-chain surface, and today’s guards don’t cover it.”

title: Mousey city-builder Whiskerwood gets a bit wetter today with a hefty nautical update that lets your rodent kingdom venture out on the open seas
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Watch out for pirats

You like putting a bunch of mice on a boat, don't you? Of course you do, it's always enjoyable seeing semi-anthropomorphic mice do human things! Now that we're on the same page, this is a good time to let you know that the new update for Whiskerwood, a city-builder where the cities are filled with mice ruled by nasty, greedy cats, has received a new update today where the friendly rodents can venture out to sail the seven seas.

Appropriately titled the Nautical Update, this one's all about boats, boat battles, ships, shipyards, trading, and more. As explained in a Steam blog post, the devs over at Minakata Dynamics consider this to be the second act of the game, the first act being the inhabitants of your city coming to terms with living under the rule of those aforementioned cats, the Claws. Prior to this update you were just focused on the one little island you inhabited, but now you'll be able to go out and see the world.

"In doing so, you'll encounter Pirates, whose threat slowly wears away at the Claw's colony system," the blog post explains. "These lawless Pirates smuggle and pillage from the Colonies and challenge the Claw's nautical supremacy. Either willingly or by force, your actions will feed the pirates. In turn, the Pirate Wars will bring the Claws to acts of desperation, acts which will grant you the schematics to outfit a navy!"

Getting the map is quite literal, as the whole thing shows you a 2D, grid-based map where you choose where you want your ships to go. Along the way you can take part in battles, or you can fish, and on certain islands you'll be able to trade goods to build up your personal supply of resources. On top of this, "keeping your crew alive is vital, as not just any Whisker can crew a ship. Only Whiskers with the new skills of Sailor or Officer can set sail. Larger ships require Officers & Sailors, while smaller ships can make do with only Sailors."

Plus on top of this, your home island can get attacked too, so you need to be prepared to defend it while you're out on your adventures. A fairly hefty sounding update! And the game's 50% off for a little while too, so, can't go wrong really. You can check it out on Steam here.

title: Koorui G2741L review
author: @pcgamer
content:
A reasonably priced 4K offering that is well worth considering on a budget. But OLED is an elephant in the room at practically the same price, and dual-mode still isn't perfect yet.

For

  • 4K and 1080p
  • Sweet IPS panel
  • Competitive pricing

Against

  • Dual-mode still not perfect
  • That's now OLED pricing

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Dual-mode is still not perfect in gaming monitors, but we are consistently getting the option for nearly no extra cost, and that is making it a mighty viable choice, especially if you are running a rig that can only sometimes run the native resolution.

The option to flit from 1080p at double the refresh rate for competitive or highly intensive games, and then back to 4K for lush sights or just a clean desktop in only a few seconds, and with native resolutions, makes so much sense to me. Koorui manages to offer both dual-mode and aggressive 4K pricing at the same time.

It's been more than a year since our review, but the Asus ROG Strix XG27UCG, which sits as our pick for the best budget 4K gaming monitor, is $100 more and offers almost identical specs. That's a few ticks in my book already.

But stats don't tell you absolutely everything; I've had this Koorui gaming monitor planted on my desk for a few weeks, and I was pleasantly surprised by it.

Buy if…

✅ You want cheap 4K with good 1080p: You would struggle to find quite so reasonable a deal on such a high refresh rate dual-mode 4K monitor.

Don't buy if…

❌ You can't run 4K: For that price, I'd be picking up a 1080p/1440p monitor, or going a little upward and getting the eye-popping colours of an OLED.

A reasonably priced 4K offering that is well worth considering on a budget. But OLED is an elephant in the room at practically the same price, and dual-mode still isn't perfect yet.

Features

In most of its basic specs, the Koorui G2741L fits the mould for a budget-oriented 4K gaming monitor. Koorui claims a 1 ms response time and 160 Hz refresh rate in 4K. It makes compromises where it needs to, being not massively bright and not super fast, but good enough in both categories to work just fine for 4K gaming. The 400 nits brightness (in HDR mode) is slightly above budget spec, though, which makes it bright enough for gaming beside a window.

The only place I might have expected even more compromises is in the size, perhaps going down to 24 inches, but then that's small enough that 4K likely isn't worth the price bump and performance hit—4K monitors smaller than 27 inches are quite rare for that reason. 27 inches is a sweet spot for dual-mode monitors, being big enough to get value out of the super high resolution, and small enough that 1080p doesn't feel like a massive hit.

Image 1 of 4

It's super easy to set up too. The monitor comes in two parts, the panel and the stand, which clip together in mere moments. Despite this being very easy, it's not a weak stand, and my desk shaking does not cause anything to pop out of place.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

You're getting two HDMI ports here, plus a DisplayPort port and an audio jack. that makes it a decent pick for a console and PC at the same time, or as a spare for your laptop when you need a second screen. You get no built-in speakers here or a USB port for charging, which is a slight shame but understandable given the cost.

The monitor itself can pivot 90 degrees to the left and right, making it a solid pick for both vertical and horizontal use. It can also tilt up to 25 degrees, and the stand holds it in place firmly.

Dual-mode is the standout feature here. You can swap from 4K to 1080p in just a few seconds with the button on the back. As it only has one button, you do have to scroll through menus, and I'd personally love a single button for activating dual-mode quickly, but it doesn't take too long to activate once you know where the button is.

Performance

Being an IPS panel, you're getting a strong viewing angle, good colours, and consistent performance. The HDR400 rating is pretty barebones, but in practice, it's punchy and feels rather bright. In fact, the monitor seemed rather stale without HDR on, and that's down to how day and night it feels. With 95% DCI-P3 colour coverage and 100% sRGB, its colour accuracy is lush for the price, though obviously it lacks the true blacks and vibrant colours of an OLED.

Though there are the typical 'not quite black' blacks of an IPS here, the contrast is strong, and made stronger thanks to the monitor's software. Mine needed very little tweaking out of the box, though I did up the contrast and brightness just a touch. I'll get into it more in the software section, but I'd advise not tweaking it too much, as it's pretty finely tuned already.

Generally speaking, using the desktop day-to-day is best in 4K, as it's not super intensive, but the smoothness of text and even just casual video really pop here. Then, picking between 4K and 1080p for gaming is largely reliant on whether or not your rig can actually handle it. In my RTX 4070 Super machine, I'd almost always opt for the higher resolution, occasionally with a helping hand from upscaling or frame gen. However, my RTX 2070 rig benefitted from being able to swap at a moment's notice. It is worth noting that 1440p is still a very solid resolution, especially at this panel size, as it still offers a solid pixel density. Therefore, there's a good reason to consider a monitor with a native 1440p output.

Image 1 of 2

Koorui has gone for a matte anti-glare coating here, which makes it slightly more viable near a window letting in a lot of light, but glossy finishes tend to offer a clearer image.

Control looks phenomenal in 4K, its angular brutalist architecture contrasting against all the blood and moody lighting. Even without true blacks, the G2741L does a great job at contrasting blacks, reds and blues, with little clarity getting lost in high-contrast scenes. The RTX 2070 can handle it at 4K, though with lower graphical settings. That's the beauty of dual-mode, though; you can bump up the textures, get a higher FPS, or just get a higher refresh rate quickly by cutting the resolution by a quarter.

Dual-mode is still, however, in somewhat of an infancy stage. I find the Koorui's 1080p performance to be just fine in the majority of games, but there's a slight fringing and softness to text on the desktop that isn't quite as present in native 1080p gaming monitors. If I were purely going for 1080p, I'd be picking a dedicated, much cheaper 1080p gaming monitor instead. It's not quite a 'best of both worlds' situation, but it's the best of 4K at its price and pretty good 1080p. Though that's not quite as catchy.

For gaming, the monitor feels plenty snappy to me, with it being decently responsive. Naturally, IPS panels are more limited than say OLEDs in terms of response time, but I wouldn't call it slow.

Dual-mode does take a few seconds to swap over, though, and you may have to exit your game and go back in, but Windows swaps resolution without any prompting. Generally, it's not a major inconvenience to swap to 1080p when I want high frame rates in Fortnite and then swap to 4K for lush sights in Cyberpunk 2077's Night City.

Aesthetics

Image 1 of 3

The Koorui is a gaming monitor, and its stand suggests as much. It's angular with red trimming, and not particularly subtle. However, with no RGB and no ugly branding slapped on the side, it looks pretty sweet to my eyes. Not understated but not loud either.

The bezels aren't super trim, but they don't distract from the gorgeous sights of 4K in between them, and the build quality is solid for the price too.

It does have a fairly wide panel and rather large base, which may make it struggle on smaller desks, but I'd wager smaller desks wouldn't be looking for 27 inches anyway. It has a VESA connector should you want to connect it to a monitor arm too.

Koorui does use a lot of plastic in the monitor, as you might expect from the price, but it doesn't feel flimsy, and it looks solid too.

Software

I suspect the OSD picks its size on the screen based on resolution, as it's oddly small in 4K. Not so small it's unusable, but certainly not as big and upfront as the 1080p version. Though it's easy to navigate, dual-mode takes a few more button clicks than I'd personally want.

You are getting a whole pile of fairly superfluous options in the OSD, like a crosshair mode that, well, adds a crosshair in the middle of the screen. Personally, this seems niche at best and distracting at worst, so I'd never use it.

You also get a DCR mode that automatically adjusts brightness and contrast based on what's on your screen. This is neat in principle but, in practice, it feels like the monitor is constantly adjusting brightness and contrast, which is just a little annoying. You get all the settings you would otherwise expect here, like brightness, contrast, an HDR game/movie mode, plus other tweaks like the overdrive mode, but it's plenty snappy, bright, and vibrant in HDR game mode, which is where I'd leave it. I mostly just used the software dual-mode, as it's not particularly laggy or hard to navigate.

Value

Though the MSRP is $350, the G2741L regularly hangs around the $250 to $300 mark. I look after our roundup of the best cheap gaming monitor deals every week, and this price tag puts it at around the same place as the MSI MAG 275UPD, which offers similar specs but a lower refresh rate.

It is around $100 more than the Acer Nitro VG270K L1, which is also a dual-mode 4K monitor, but the Acer panel offers a very limiting 72 Hz refresh rate in 4K. That's all to say that the G2741L is very competitively priced, hanging around the lowest-cost 4K panels right now.

If I were looking for a 4K monitor, this Koorui would no doubt be on my list. If I had exactly $250-$300, I can't think of anything I'd be picking over it.

But there's an elephant in the room here, and that's OLED. OLED gaming monitors have become such good value recently that budget 4K IPS panels are sitting around the budget OLED price point, and that opportunity cost is fierce. For instance, the gorgeous 1440p Alienware AW2726DM comes in at the same price point, and though its max refresh rate and resolution are lower, you are getting the true blacks of an OLED, plus super snappy response times too.

As is ever the case, the biggest problem with gaming monitors right now is that there are too many choices, but Koorui has successfully made that decision even harder.

Koorui G2741L review

A reasonably priced 4K offering that is well worth considering on a budget. But OLED is an elephant in the room at practically the same price, and dual-mode still isn't perfect yet.

James is a more recent PC gaming convert, often admiring graphics cards, cases, and motherboards from afar. It was not until 2019, after just finishing a degree in law and media, that they decided to throw out the last few years of education, build their PC, and start writing about gaming instead. In that time, he has covered the latest doodads, contraptions, and gismos, and loved every second of it. Hey, it’s better than writing case briefs.

title: Sony's discless PlayStation PR disaster isn't going away, as State of Play once again flooded with protests about discs and Destiny 3 from angered fans
author: Connor Makar
content:
"No disc no buy."

Today's Sony State of Play livestream was packed full of new game trailers, reveals, and announcements for PlayStation fans. However, if you took a look at the live chat, you'll have mostly just seen two groups of angered fans clamouring after discs and Destiny.

Messages like "NO DISC NO BUY" and "WE WANT DESTINY 3" were spammed during the State of Play, from start to finish, in the YouTube live chat. Popping over the Twitch, that stream was endlessly spammed by Destiny emotes, and similar calls for a physical game support.

In case you missed it, this outrage is a collision between two separate PR disasters for Sony. The first is tied to Sony's announcement that physical game support will stop starting in 2028, meaning only digital codes will be available for games on its platform starting in January of that year.

This proved immediately controversial, though Sony has pledged to stay the course despite the palpable anger from PlayStation players. It even recently argued that "reasonable consumers" know they don't actually own the digital games they buy in an ongoing class action lawsuit.

The second controversy stems from the end of major support for Destiny 2 and major staffing cuts at Bungie. Despite a resurgence of support from Destiny 2 players in the wake of this news, Bungie seems committed to Marathon despite its struggles. As a result, fans are pushing hard for Destiny 3 despite how seemingly unlikely it is to be greenlit.

With regards to PlayStation's discless future, outcry on social media has persisted ever since that announcement. Even if the data suggests the vast majority of purchases are made in digital form rather than physical, the strength of feeling here is significant, which many would argue is for good reason. These protests will likely remain a problem for Sony for some time.

title: Elephants Think Before They Act - Nautilus
content:
As humans, we value rational decision-making in which we resist impulses to make better decisions. This “inhibitory control” is also found in other primates and some birds. Such ability to self-regulate is not, however, known in elephants. Will an elephant, for example, grab a proffered banana even if it means missing out on a better meal later on?

Featured Video

In a study published today in the journal PLOS One, a team of researchers from Thailand and the U.S. studied impulse control in Asian elephants (Elephas maximus). In particular, they presented a problem-solving task to 16 elephants (eight males and eight females), housed at the National Elephant Institute in Thailand. 

Read more: “How Hannibal’s War Elephants Helped to Determine His Route Through the Alps”

First, the elephants were trained to reach with their trunks around a black plastic box to pull a favored fruit out of an opening on the back (either pineapple, apple, or banana, depending on the individual elephant). Next, the elephants were presented with a transparent box that had small front-facing holes, too small to reach through but large enough for the fruit odors to waft out. To access the fruit, they’d still need to reach around the back.

You’d expect an impulsive elephant to try to grab the visible, fragrant fruit from the front. Instead, all the elephants reached around the box, just as they had on the black training box. Even when the orientation of the box was changed, such that the accessible opening was upward or to one side, elephants uncovered the fruit in less than a minute.

“We found that, when elephants were faced with a situation where they needed to suppress an impulsive behavior—either the impulse to reach directly toward a food reward behind a transparent and perforated barrier, or the impulse to continue using a previously (but no longer) effective technique—they were generally able to suppress the impulse,” said the study authors in a press release.

That said, older elephants were slower at adjusting to new orientations of the box, which may indicate an age-related limitation such as cognitive decline. The study authors wrote that “this is consistent with studies in other species that have found inhibitory control declines with age.” 

But overall, they seemed more than capable of adhering to one of the oldest lessons in the book: to think before acting.

title: Why Is Everyone In Tech So Sad?
author: Krista Stevens
content:
If you spend your day in front of a computer, you may ask yourself, at times, why you do it. What’s it all for? Who benefits? For Noēma, Aaron Horwath suggests that the crisis confronting knowledge workers these days isn’t strictly economic, it’s also existential. He explores the pitfalls of work-as-performance and wonders whether the “messy middle,” which embraces human interaction and collaboration over an army of agents, might offer more for workers and employers alike.

But perhaps the most powerful action of all is simply to maintain an awareness (and remind others) that Workism is a spectacle. For most employees, we owe it to each other to remind one another that this work is not, in the grand scheme of things, all that important. It is illusory. No one has ever died over a spreadsheet. The world does not wait with bated breath for product launches. A marketing campaign will not change the world. Almost no one will remember all the work we do. But they might remember the types of people we were, the relationships we had and how we treated the people we worked with.

title: Can You Write a Memoir in the Third Person?
author: @NewYorker
content:
“A boy stands at the crossroads, considers his limited options.” The opening line of Brian Dillon’s memoir, “Ambivalence: An Education,” maps a juncture familiar to many. As a teen-ager in Ireland in the nineteen-eighties, Dillon toggled between constant states of panic and boredom, hoping to avoid the strictures of a conventional life style and, consequently, the moribund, mainstream tastes that come with it. A precocious reader and thinker, the young Dillon grows enamored with the radical possibilities of style. He’s not just a fan of David Bowie; he thinks of Bowie as an orientation, a world view. Yet he is bedevilled by insecurity, easily undone when mocked by schoolmates for his geeky devotions to the pop charts or science fiction. He’s in for a solitary journey, toward “the promise of escape, the promise of promise itself.”

The overheated circuits of teen-age life are well-worn ground for a coming-of-age story, yet Dillon’s approach is anything but. The writer and editor has become known for a kind of memoir-inflected approach to criticism, publishing a series of entrancing books that are as much about questions of form and technique as they are about art’s power to move and transform. In recent works such as “Suppose a Sentence” (an examination of twenty-seven perfect sentences) or “Essayism” (a free-associative attempt to tease, stretch, and swerve around the boundaries of essay-writing), Dillon wanders through his shelves, scrutinizing works by Walter Benjamin, Joan Didion, or James Baldwin and seeing, at a granular level, how writing achieves such profound effects. “Ambivalence” isn’t a how-I-did-it prehistory of his career, as it ends well before he published anything of note. Rather, he writes about this formative span of his late teens and early twenties in the third person, investigating the passions and neuroses of young “B” from a distance. Few people intervene on B’s trajectory, if you can call it that; he spends most of his days dreaming and turning newly discovered ideas over in his mind until they feel like his own. Trauma and tragedies—such as the death of his parents, or periods of estrangement from his siblings—receive less scrutiny than the emotions unlocked by Virginia Woolf or Roland Barthes. The result is a strange, bewitching experiment in autobiography, in which there are no friendships or love affairs, just exquisite digressions on life-changing texts.

Memoirs rely on a balance of the singular and the universal. We are curious about the idiosyncrasies of another’s life, but they can’t be so idiosyncratic that the reader finds their passions or motives wholly unrelatable. The all-knowing first person can suggest that a memoirist has already made sense of everything before sitting down to write: all the details and detours have been assimilated into a single, overarching story. Yet this isn’t how life feels in the moment, and Dillon attempts to capture the texture of a stretch of youth where nothing seems to be happening quickly enough. Viewing B as a kind of specimen allows the teen-ager to meander and fumble of his own volition, free of the adult’s earned wisdoms. He only understands the feeling of need, as is the self-obsessive wont of the teen. But B hasn’t yet figured out how to put any of these desires into language. Even years later, it’s as though the brooding young man can’t truly be known.

There is a rough narrative shape here, with the account beginning shortly after the death of Dillon’s mother and ending as he moves to England to pursue his graduate studies. He was a bright child but never an academic superstar—not that he was motivated, per se, by status or career. B goes through the motions of his life in clipped fragments of prose, as if to mimic the raw intensities that drive him. But occasionally Dillon steps in and muses about the broader contexts just out of focus to the young. Having failed to get into college, B enrolls at a school for “disappointed university applicants” to pass the time before reapplication. B feels that his dreams might be vanishing, yet Dillon reminds us that he is still too young to surrender them:

The future exists as a figment or mirage, that is when it is not bearing on him like a threat or demand. He has not yet in life (unlike imagination) spied an ambition or goal, settled on a course of action to achieve it, then carried this through with doggedness or aplomb. He understands decisions must be made, whether by him or for him, but he has no conception of those decisions turning out to be the right ones, leading to this or that desired outcome. This is not only because, from the place and time where he lives, everything he cares about feels remote and fantastical, a migrainous shimmer at the edges of vision, impossible to bring into focus. Just as implausible: the real world of study, employment, making one’s way . . . The dull enigma of when you are older and when you have a job. In the hours when he is not overtaken by pure desire, love, or loneliness, he seems to exist mostly as a tide of reverie, with undertows of avoidance and boredom. This is not a completely unpleasant way to be.

The first-person insights of memoir serve epiphany and discovery, as though all confessions are truthful. The distance of third person makes these moments of reflection more meaningful, as though part of the book’s journey is young B’s discovery of a language that might capture how he feels inside. Occasionally, Dillon writes in the second person, addressing B directly but also universalizing the young man’s plight. “Always on your mind is the prospect of wasting your life, which means doing what you are told and doing it poorly, but well enough to find, in time, a job and a station in life that will blight all ambitions and all attachments to art, language, thought, desire.” These are moments for us to wander into the text and measure ourselves against his fire.

“Ambivalence” is set between 1986 and 1995, a time when Dillon was “always imagining how things will be in about six months’ time: how he will dress, how he will speak and move in the world, what adjustments he will have made to his character and how he will be understood by others—perhaps even loved.” There were other important people in his life during this span—a path-changing academic mentor, a torturous sibling, his father—but the engine of “Ambivalence” is his personal syllabus. He reads Virginia Woolf’s “The Waves,” and, as he falls into the text’s dizzying similes and metaphors, he grows infatuated with the “richness of substitution, conjuring one thing out of another, proving all things subtly or strangely not themselves. This is also that.” Descriptions of lovers or of his best friend, “S,” feel hazy and thin, yet he ponders at length about what passage from the book he wants read aloud at his funeral, rather than who will be in attendance.

All criticism is autobiographical, in the sense that it clues a reader in to the touchstones or influences that make a given critic’s taste unique. Dillon’s unusual approach throughout “Ambivalence” slowly comes into focus when B becomes hypnotized by the tenets of postmodernity, such as the mutability of the self, or the impossibility of fixed truths: if we are always works in progress, rather than stable selves awaiting discovery, then the most truthful account of one’s life would be one that denies discrete turning points or the grand illusion of ever being fully formed. Dillon’s fondness for italicized phrases and his occasionally grave tone are all part of a performance, something that he has learned from reading French theory. The very look of Barthes’s and Derrida’s writings inspires a way of living, “a dream of italicizing everything, inflecting every utterance, making language and life lean away from the solid, upright and reasonable. Obliquity is everything.”

B grows fixated on the “subjective, vulnerable, unmastered” style of Barthes, as the French thinker’s approach to essay writing “splintered” into something messy and strange, working through evocation and juxtaposition rather than persuasion. The closest “Ambivalence” comes to breakthrough is when B realizes that writing is where you figure these things out, even if the resulting essay is shaggy and abstruse. At one point, he is comfortably settled in graduate school, measuring his perception of self against how he seems to others. “Later he will learn that some of his fellow postgraduate students think he is pretentious, and he will feel amused, gratified, properly seen at last.” He wonders if he could ever fall in love with someone who does not read Derrida. Probably not.

For many years, I taught a writing workshop on cultural criticism that began with students composing a taste biography. What were the pivotal encounters that shaped their sense of what art could be and how it might affect them? Was it always love at first sight? We talked about the difference between merely liking a film and allowing it to transform you, the aspirations we might have to one day understand something we currently find difficult or unruly.

I still believe that the songs or books we love contain blueprints for how we hope to live, and Dillon’s memoir embodies how these personal canons inflect the way we understand and express ourselves. B fears being outed as a poseur, meekly copying the outline of some micro clique, rather than a true aesthete “driven only by curiosity and love.” Fifty pages in, the author observes that he has “not yet, in any meaningful sense of the verbs, begun to read—or write.”

You’ll drift in and out of “Ambivalence,” and muse on your own formative inputs. As I turned the pages, wondering whether any of B’s quandaries would be resolved, the book reminded me of how much of youth is spent pondering time, waiting, ready for the world beyond and yet slightly terrified of what’s actually out there. It’s an ode to a kind of boredom that feels desperate, endless, and, in retrospect, luxurious.

I’m about a decade younger than Dillon, and I recognized his desire to hoard and paw at any morsel connecting his small world to an alternative culture somewhere out there. As a child of the nineties, I at least had the benefit of cable television and the early days of dial-up internet. But I’m closer in age to Dillon than to those currently in their teens and early twenties; I wonder if Dillon’s dream of accumulation (of books, songs, ideas, anything), redolent of the eighties and nineties, still holds in an age of far too much. Do people still have the spare hours to linger and obsess over the meaning of taste, when the internet delivers us an endless stream of ready-made new poses? “Ambivalence” is a story of solitude, patience, and faith—qualities that contemporary culture seems to militate against. One of my favorite moments comes when an excited classmate emerges from the library holding a new book of feminist literary theory. “I have no fucking clue what it’s about,” B’s friend says, “but it’s brilliant.” There’s still time to figure out what it all means. ♦
